followups.a: The answer only improves when a larger maxFreq appears. A stale, too-large value can make the window seem valid for longer, but it can never produce a window longer than the best genuinely achievable one, because that would require a real maxFreq at least as large.
Record the left index whenever the window length improves.

learnings.insight: The canonical sliding window. The window is valid while it holds no duplicate, and the corrective move on a duplicate is to advance the left edge past the previous occurrence - not by one, which would be O(n^2) in the worst case.
learnings.trick: Store last-seen index per character. On seeing a repeat inside the window, jump l = max(l, lastSeen[c] + 1). The max() is essential - a stale occurrence outside the window must not drag l backwards.
edge_cases: Without max(), 'abba' gives a wrong answer: the second 'a' pulls l back behind 'b'.
Empty string returns 0.
Use int last[128] for ASCII rather than a hash map - faster and O(1) space.

complexity.why: each index is visited once by each pointer and l never retreats. The O(n^2) all-substrings check is what this replaces.

followups.a: lastSeen may point to an occurrence already left behind. Without max, l jumps backwards, re-admitting characters that were correctly excluded.

followups.q: At most k distinct characters instead of zero repeats.
followups.a: A frequency map plus a shrink condition on map size. LC 340, the premium version, but Fruit Into Baskets is the free k = 2 case.

followups.q: Return the substring rather than its length.
followups.a: Record the left index whenever the best length improves.

learnings.insight: Nesting means the most recently opened bracket must close first, which is precisely a stack's contract. Any problem describing nesting is a stack problem before you have read the second paragraph.
learnings.trick: Push openers. On a closer, fail if the stack is empty or the top does not match. After the loop, the stack MUST be empty - forgetting that check lets '(((' pass.
edge_cases: Unclosed brackets - caught only by the final emptiness test.
A closer arriving on an empty stack must fail, not be ignored.
Odd-length input can be rejected immediately as a micro-optimisation.

complexity.why: one pass, with the stack holding at most n openers. No cleverness reduces the space, since fully nested input genuinely requires remembering every opener.

followups.a: A counter suffices - increment on open, decrement on close, fail if it goes negative. O(1) space. Multiple types are what force the stack.
LC 32 - a stack of INDICES, or a two-pass counter sweep from both directions. Genuinely harder than the validity check.

tuf.striver_title: Add two numbers in Linked List

learnings.insight: The digits are stored least-significant-first, which is exactly the order addition needs. A dummy head removes the special case of creating the first result node, and handling the carry after the loop removes the special case of a final carry.
learnings.trick: Loop while either list remains OR the carry is non-zero. Inside, sum the two values plus carry, append sum % 10, and set carry = sum / 10.
edge_cases: A final carry creates an extra node - 5 + 5 = [0,1]. Including `|| carry` in the loop condition handles it.
Lists of different lengths - treat a missing node as 0.
Empty lists - the dummy head means the result is correctly null-ish.

complexity.why: one pass over the longer list. No extra space beyond the result, which is unavoidable.

followups.a: LC 445 - either reverse both lists, add, and reverse the result, or push onto two stacks and build the answer from the front. The stack version avoids mutating the input.

followups.q: Why include `|| carry` in the loop condition?
followups.a: Otherwise a carry generated by the last pair of digits is dropped, and 5 + 5 returns [0] instead of [0,1].

learnings.insight: On a straight path a faster runner simply disappears ahead. On a circular one they must eventually lap the slower runner. So meeting is equivalent to the existence of a cycle - and it needs no memory at all.
learnings.trick: slow advances one, fast advances two. Guard with `while (fast && fast->next)` because fast dereferences two links per step.
edge_cases: The guard must check both fast and fast->next, or you dereference null on even-length acyclic lists.
A single node pointing to itself is a cycle.
Empty list has no cycle.

complexity.why: fast closes the gap by one node per step inside the cycle, so they meet within cycle-length steps of slow entering it. A hash set of visited nodes is also O(n) time but O(n) space.

followups.q: Why must they meet rather than pass each other?
followups.a: Inside the cycle the gap shrinks by exactly one each step, so it reaches zero - it can never jump from one to minus one.
Hold one pointer at the meeting point and advance the other until they coincide again, counting steps.
LC 142 - reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time.

tuf.striver_title: Find the starting point in LL

learnings.insight: After the pointers meet, resetting one to the head and advancing both at the same speed brings them together exactly at the cycle entry. The proof is short and interviewers ask for it, so learn it rather than the code.
learnings.trick: Detect the meeting as in LC 141, then set slow = head and advance both one step at a time until they are equal. That node is the entry.
edge_cases: The reset must happen at the meeting point, not after any further movement.
No cycle means returning nullptr - handle it before the second phase.
The entry may be the head itself, which the algorithm handles naturally.

complexity.why: two linear phases. The hash-set solution is simpler but O(n) space, and this problem exists specifically to rule it out.

followups.a: Let k be the tail length and c the cycle length. When slow enters the cycle it has walked k and fast has walked 2k, so fast is k into the cycle. They meet k mod c before the entry. A pointer from the head needs k steps to the entry; the meeting pointer needs k too, walking k mod c plus whole loops. They arrive together.
LC 287: with values in [1,n] treat a[i] as a next-pointer. The duplicate is the cycle entry. That disguise is the single highest-leverage one in DSA.

tuf.striver_title: Check if LL is palindrome or not

learnings.insight: Copying values into an array makes this trivial but costs O(n) space. The O(1) solution composes two techniques you already have - find the middle with fast/slow, then reverse the second half in place and walk the two halves together.
learnings.trick: Find the middle, reverse from there, compare until the reversed half runs out, then reverse it back so the caller's list is unmodified.
edge_cases: Restoring the list afterwards is what separates a careful answer from a passing one.
Odd length leaves a middle node that belongs to neither half and is skipped.
Empty and single-node lists are palindromes.

complexity.why: three linear phases - find middle, reverse, compare. The array-copy solution is the same time but O(n) space.

followups.a: Say yes and point at the line. Mutating a caller's structure without restoring it is a genuine defect, not a stylistic quibble.

followups.q: Why compare until the reversed half ends rather than the first?
followups.a: The first half may be one node longer when the length is odd. Terminating on the shorter side skips the unpaired middle automatically.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

tuf.striver_title: Remove Nth node from the back of the LL

learnings.insight: You cannot index backwards in a singly linked list, but you can open a fixed gap between two pointers and walk them together. When the leader hits the end, the follower is exactly n from it.
learnings.trick: Start BOTH pointers at a dummy head, advance fast by n, then advance both until fast->next is null. Slow now sits on the node BEFORE the target, which is what you need to unlink it.
edge_cases: Removing the head itself is why the dummy exists - without it, n == length is a special case.
Starting both at the dummy rather than the head is what makes slow land on the predecessor.
n is guaranteed valid, so no bounds check is needed.

complexity.why: one pass. The two-pass version measuring the length first is equally O(n) and arguably clearer - say which you chose and why.

followups.a: Measure the length, then walk length - n steps. Simpler to reason about; the one-pass version is what the follow-up asks for.

followups.q: Why start at the dummy rather than the head?
followups.a: It shifts slow back by one so it lands on the predecessor instead of the target, and it makes removing the head identical to removing anything else.

learnings.insight: Three pointers and a strict order of operations. Every harder list problem - reverse in groups, palindrome check, reorder - contains this loop, so getting it automatic pays for itself many times over.
learnings.trick: Save next BEFORE rewiring, because cur->next is about to be destroyed. Then point cur at prev, and advance both. Return prev, not cur - cur ends at nullptr.
edge_cases: Empty list returns nullptr; the loop simply does not execute.
Single node returns itself.
Returning cur instead of prev is the classic slip - cur is null when the loop exits.

complexity.why: one pass rewiring each pointer once. The recursive version is also O(n) time but O(n) stack, which matters at 1e5 nodes.

followups.a: Recurse to the end, then on the way back set head->next->next = head and head->next = nullptr. Elegant, but O(n) stack - say so.

followups.q: Reverse only positions m to n.
followups.a: LC 92 - use a dummy head, walk to m-1, then splice nodes to the front of the sublist one at a time. The dummy is what removes the m = 1 special case.

learnings.insight: Merge sort is the right algorithm for a linked list specifically because it never needs random access, and because merging relinks nodes rather than copying them - giving O(1) auxiliary space beyond the recursion stack.
learnings.trick: Split with fast/slow, cutting the list by setting prev->next = nullptr. Recurse on both halves, then merge with a dummy head.
edge_cases: The split MUST sever the first half, or the recursion never terminates.
A single node or empty list is the base case.
Recursion depth is O(log n), which is safe; a bottom-up iterative merge gives true O(1) space.

complexity.why: log n levels of recursion with O(n) merging each. Quick sort on a list needs O(n) to find a pivot and partitions awkwardly, which is why it is not used here.

followups.a: Bottom-up merge sort: merge sublists of size 1, then 2, then 4, iterating rather than recursing. No stack at all.
Pivot selection is O(n) without random access, and partitioning a list requires rebuilding chains. Merge sort's split is O(n) but its merge is natural for linked structures.

learnings.insight: Identical to Next Greater Element, but the answer is a DISTANCE rather than a value - which is precisely why the stack must hold indices. This is the problem that teaches you never to store values in a monotonic stack.
learnings.trick: Decreasing stack of indices. When the current temperature exceeds the one at the stack top, the answer for that index is i - stackTop.
edge_cases: Store indices, not temperatures, or the distance is unrecoverable.
Indices never popped keep their default answer of 0.
Equal temperatures do not count as warmer - use strict comparison.

complexity.why: each index is pushed and popped once. The pairwise scan is O(n^2) and is what this replaces.

followups.q: Solve it right to left instead.
followups.a: Walk backwards with an increasing stack, popping anything not warmer. Equivalent, and some find the direction more intuitive.

followups.q: The temperature range is bounded at 30 to 100.
followups.a: That permits an O(n * 71) solution tracking the next occurrence of each temperature - worse in theory, but it shows you noticed the constraint.

learnings.insight: For each bar, the widest rectangle of that height extends left to the previous shorter bar and right to the next shorter one. A single increasing stack produces both boundaries in one pass - when a bar is popped, the new top is its left boundary and the current index is its right.
learnings.trick: Append a sentinel height of 0 to force the stack to drain. Width is i - stackTopAfterPop - 1, which correctly handles the case where the stack empties.
edge_cases: Without the sentinel you need a separate drain loop after the main pass.
When the stack empties after a pop, the left boundary is -1, so width is simply i.
Equal heights can use either comparison; the maximum is unaffected.

complexity.why: each bar is pushed and popped once. The O(n^2) approach expanding from each bar is what this replaces.

followups.q: Maximal rectangle in a binary matrix.
followups.a: LC 85 - run this once per row, treating consecutive ones above each row as histogram heights. O(m*n) total.

followups.q: Why does the popped element's width extend past the current top?
followups.a: Everything between them was taller and already popped, so the popped bar's height is valid across that whole span.
Recurse on the minimum bar, O(n log n) average but O(n^2) worst on sorted input. The stack is strictly better.

learnings.insight: getMin must be O(1), which rules out scanning. The fix is to remember, alongside every element, what the minimum was at the moment it was pushed - so popping automatically restores the previous minimum.
learnings.trick: Push min(x, currentMin) onto a second stack on every push, and pop both together. No conditional logic and no risk of losing a minimum.
edge_cases: Duplicate minimums must be pushed every time, or popping one loses the other.
getMin on an empty stack is undefined - the problem guarantees valid calls.
Pushing the min unconditionally is simpler and safer than pushing only on improvement.

complexity.why: every operation is a constant number of stack operations. The auxiliary stack doubles memory, which the O(1)-space variant avoids at the cost of overflow risk.

followups.q: Do it without the second stack.
followups.a: Store 2*x - min when a new minimum arrives, and recover the previous minimum on pop. It works but can overflow, so it is worth naming rather than implementing.

followups.q: A max stack with the same guarantees.
followups.a: Symmetric. A stack supporting both min and max needs two auxiliary stacks or one of pairs.
Requires an ordered structure alongside the stack - a multiset plus a doubly linked list. That is LC 716.

learnings.insight: To make a number as small as possible, remove a digit whenever it is followed by a smaller one - that swap lowers a more significant place. A monotonic increasing stack performs exactly those removals greedily.
learnings.trick: Maintain an increasing stack, popping while the top exceeds the incoming digit and removals remain. If k is still positive at the end, drop from the back. Strip leading zeros last.
edge_cases: Leftover k after the pass means the digits were already increasing - remove from the END.
Leading zeros must be stripped, and an empty result becomes '0'.
k equal to the length returns '0'.

complexity.why: each digit is pushed and popped once. The combinatorial choice of which k digits to remove is exponential, which is what the greedy replaces.

followups.a: If d[i] > d[i+1], removing d[i] reduces the digit at the most significant differing position, which dominates every lower place. So it is never worse to remove it.
Flip the stack direction to decreasing. Same algorithm.

followups.q: Remove duplicate letters keeping lexicographic minimality.
followups.a: LC 316 - same monotonic stack, plus a last-occurrence table so you never pop a letter that will not reappear.

learnings.insight: A heap gives O(n log k) but cannot cheaply remove elements leaving the window. A monotonic deque can, because any element smaller than a later arrival is permanently irrelevant and can be discarded immediately.
learnings.trick: Deque of indices with decreasing values. Evict from the front when the index falls out of the window; evict from the back while the new value dominates. The front is always the window maximum.
edge_cases: Store indices so the out-of-window check is possible.
Front eviction must come before back eviction to keep the window valid.
Start recording answers only once i >= k-1.

complexity.why: each index is pushed and popped exactly once, so the two inner whiles contribute O(n) in total. The heap solution is O(n log k) with lazy deletion.

followups.q: Why is a smaller earlier element permanently irrelevant?
followups.a: It leaves the window no later than the larger newer one, and it is smaller, so it can never be the maximum while the newer element is present.
The deque trick does not apply - medians need order statistics. Use two heaps with lazy deletion, or a multiset with an iterator to the middle. LC 480.
Flip the comparison. The deque becomes increasing.

learnings.insight: Do not enumerate subarrays. Count each element's CONTRIBUTION: a[i] is the minimum of exactly left * right subarrays, where left is the distance to the previous smaller element and right the distance to the next smaller. That reframing is the whole problem.
learnings.trick: Two monotonic stack passes give previous-smaller and next-smaller boundaries. Answer is the sum of a[i] * left * right, taken modulo 1e9+7.
edge_cases: Duplicates must use strict comparison on one side and non-strict on the other, or identical subarrays are counted twice.
Products overflow int - accumulate in long long and reduce modulo at each step.
Elements with no smaller neighbour extend to the array boundary.

complexity.why: two linear stack passes. Enumerating all subarrays is O(n^2) and exceeds the limits.

followups.a: If both sides used strict comparison, a subarray whose minimum appears twice would be counted for each occurrence. Making one side non-strict assigns it to exactly one.
LC 2104 - run the same computation for maxima and subtract the minima total. Two applications of one idea.

learnings.insight: 'Two baskets' is 'at most two distinct values in the window' wearing a story. Stripping the narrative to the constraint is the actual skill - and once stripped, it is a textbook variable window with a frequency map.
learnings.trick: Expand right, incrementing the count for the new fruit. While the map holds more than two keys, advance left and ERASE any key whose count reaches zero - otherwise map.size() is wrong.
edge_cases: Erasing zero-count keys is mandatory; without it the size check never triggers correctly.
Fewer than three distinct fruits overall means the answer is the whole array.
The answer is a count of fruits, which is the window length.

complexity.space: O(1) since at most three keys are ever held
complexity.why: each index enters and leaves once. The map holds at most k+1 entries, so its operations are effectively constant.

followups.a: Replace 2 with k. That is LC 340, which is premium - this problem is the free instance of it.

followups.q: Why must zero-count keys be erased?
followups.a: unordered_map::size() counts keys, not non-zero values. A key left at zero keeps inflating the distinct count and the window never shrinks correctly.

learnings.insight: The definitive example of the atMost decomposition. A window for exactly k distinct values has no valid shrink rule, but atMost(k) is routine - and exactly(k) is the difference of two such counts.
learnings.trick: atMost(k) counts subarrays with at most k distinct values by accumulating (r - l + 1). Return atMost(k) - atMost(k-1).
edge_cases: Erase zero-count keys or the distinct count is wrong.
k = 1 still needs atMost(0), which must return 0.
Accumulating (r - l + 1) counts every valid subarray ending at r, not just the longest.

complexity.why: two linear passes, each with a map bounded by k+1 entries.

followups.a: Every subarray with at most k distinct values is counted once in the first term. Those with at most k-1 appear in both terms and cancel. What survives has exactly k.

followups.q: Why does accumulating (r - l + 1) count correctly?
followups.a: For a valid window [l, r], every subarray ending at r and starting at or after l is also valid, because removing elements from the left cannot increase the distinct count.

learnings.insight: Split the data into a lower half and an upper half, each kept as a heap facing inward. The median then sits at the tops. The difficulty is not the idea but keeping the invariant that every element in the lower half is at most every element in the upper.
learnings.trick: Always push to the max-heap, immediately move its top to the min-heap, then rebalance sizes if the min-heap has grown larger. Three unconditional operations, no case analysis.
edge_cases: Naively pushing to whichever heap 'looks right' breaks the ordering invariant.
Odd totals leave the extra element in the max-heap by convention.
Use double division for the even case, or integer division truncates.

complexity.time: O(log n) per insertion, O(1) per query
complexity.why: each insertion performs a constant number of heap operations. A sorted container with insertion is O(n) per add.

followups.a: A 101-slot count array plus a running total gives O(1) insertion and O(100) median - counting sort again.

followups.q: 99% of values are in a narrow range.
followups.a: Bucket the common range and keep overflow lists for outliers.
LC 480 - two heaps plus lazy deletion via a to-remove map, or a multiset with an iterator kept at the middle. Removal is what makes it substantially harder.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array

learnings.insight: Sorting is O(n log n) and answers far more than was asked. The two better options are a size-k MIN-heap at O(n log k), and quickselect at O(n) average - and knowing when each is correct is the actual question.
learnings.trick: For the k LARGEST, keep a MIN-heap of size k. The inversion is deliberate: the weakest of your current winners sits on top, ready to be evicted in O(log k).
edge_cases: k is 1-indexed; k = 1 is the maximum.
Duplicates count toward k - the 2nd largest of [3,3,1] is 3.
Pop only when the size EXCEEDS k, not when it equals k.

complexity.time: O(n log k) with the heap, O(n) average with quickselect
complexity.why: each of n elements costs O(log k) to insert and possibly evict. Quickselect recurses into only one partition, giving T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n).

followups.q: Why a min-heap for the k largest?
followups.a: You repeatedly need to discard the WORST of your current best k. A min-heap keeps that at the root; a max-heap would make finding it O(k).

followups.q: Data does not fit in memory.
followups.a: Quickselect needs random access to the whole array, so it is unavailable. The size-k heap streams and uses only O(k) space - that constraint is what decides between them.
Median-of-medians pivot selection makes quickselect worst-case linear, at the cost of a large constant that makes it slower in practice.

learnings.insight: Count first, then select. The heap gives O(n log k), but frequencies are bounded by n, which means bucket sort gives O(n) - the same instinct as counting sort, and the follow-up the question is really after.
learnings.trick: Bucket by frequency: an array of n+1 vectors indexed by count, filled from the frequency map, then read from the highest index down until k elements are collected.
edge_cases: Bucket array needs n+1 slots, since a frequency can equal n.
Ties may be returned in any order here.
Stop as soon as k elements are collected, not after draining every bucket.

complexity.time: O(n) with bucketing, O(n log k) with a heap
complexity.why: counting is linear and bucketing is linear because the frequency range is bounded. The heap version pays a log factor to avoid the extra array.

followups.a: Bucket sort by frequency. The bound on frequencies is the constraint that makes it possible - the same reasoning as counting sort.

followups.q: Top K Frequent WORDS with lexicographic tie-breaking.
followups.a: LC 692 - a heap with a custom comparator, since bucketing alone cannot order ties.
Partition the (value, count) pairs on count. O(n) average, O(1) extra space beyond the map.

learnings.insight: The wildcard makes the open-bracket count uncertain, so track a RANGE of possible counts rather than a single number. That range idea generalises to many problems with non-deterministic choices.
learnings.trick: Keep lo and hi, the minimum and maximum possible open counts. '(' increments both, ')' decrements both, '*' decrements lo and increments hi. Clamp lo at 0 and fail if hi goes negative.
edge_cases: Clamping lo at zero is essential - a negative minimum is meaningless, since '*' could have been empty.
hi < 0 means even treating every '*' as '(' cannot balance - fail immediately.
Success requires lo == 0 at the end, not merely lo <= 0.

complexity.why: one pass with two counters. The DP formulation is O(n^2) and the two-pass greedy is an equivalent alternative.

followups.a: lo counts the minimum possible open brackets. It cannot be negative, because any '*' that would have driven it negative can simply be treated as empty instead.
Scan left to right treating '*' as '(' and checking the count never goes negative, then right to left treating '*' as ')'. Both passes passing implies validity.

tuf.striver_title: Count primes in range L to R

learnings.insight: Testing each number for primality is O(n sqrt n). The sieve inverts the work - instead of asking whether each number is prime, it marks the multiples of each prime - giving O(n log log n), which is very nearly linear.
learnings.trick: Start the inner loop at i*i, not 2i: every smaller multiple of i has a factor below i and was already marked. Outer loop only while i*i <= n.
edge_cases: 0 and 1 are not prime and must be marked false explicitly.
i*i overflows int for large n - use long long in the loop bounds.
The answer counts primes strictly less than n, not up to and including it.

complexity.why: the inner loop runs n/p times per prime p, and the sum of 1/p over primes up to n is ln ln n by Mertens' theorem.

followups.a: Any multiple k*i with k < i has the smaller factor k, so it was crossed out when the sieve processed k. Starting earlier is correct but wasteful.
The linear sieve marks each composite exactly once by its smallest prime factor, and gives you that factor for free - which makes later factorisations O(log n).
Skip even numbers entirely and index only odds, or use a bitset instead of vector<bool> - though vector<bool> is already bit-packed in libstdc++.

problems.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

tuf.striver_title: Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array

learnings.insight: The O(n^2) pairwise scan is obvious. The insight that makes it O(32n) is that a trie can index BITS rather than characters - insert every number as a 32-bit path, then for each number walk greedily preferring the opposite bit at every level.
learnings.trick: Greedy works because a higher bit outweighs every lower bit combined: setting bit k gains 2^k, while all bits below sum to 2^k - 1. So take the opposite branch whenever it exists.
edge_cases: Insert all numbers before querying, or you miss pairs.
Fixed 32-bit depth regardless of the values.
Fall back to the same branch when the opposite child is absent.

complexity.why: each number is inserted and queried in 32 steps. The trie holds at most 32n nodes.

followups.q: Why is the greedy bit choice optimal?
followups.a: 2^k > 2^k - 1 = sum of all lower bits, so securing a higher bit always beats any combination of lower ones. Greedy from the top is therefore exact.
Build the answer bit by bit from the top, keeping a hash set of prefixes at each level and testing whether the desired complement exists. Same bound, no trie structure.
